extracted.intended_audience: naval timber inspectors, shipbuilders, Admiralty officials, and geographers evaluating foreign woods
extracted.subtask_description: Assessing and classifying woods from Eastern Africa, Madagascar, and the Seychelles for naval and manufacturing use, based on dimensions, specific gravity, grain, durability, and practical procurement considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class 1 woods — small dimensions but good quality (local purposes)
rubrics_metrics.description: "All those which are of small dimensions, and do not attain in their growth the size of timber-trees, but, being of good quality, may be useful for local purposes—such are Nos. 1, 2, 3, 6, 8, 9, 15, 16, 18, 19, 25, and 26."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These woods are acceptable where large sizes are not required; useful for local ship repairs, joinery or other local manufacture. Examples given (by specimen numbers) indicate relatively small scantlings but acceptable quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class 2 woods — small dimensions and inferior quality (not valuable in manufacture)
rubrics_metrics.description: "Those which are of small dimensions, and do not attain to the character of timber-trees, and, being of inferior quality, are not likely to be of any value in manufacture—such are Nos. 4, 5, 10, 11, and 14."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Woods in this class should generally be discounted for manufacturing or naval use because of both size and poor material properties; retain only for trivial/local uses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class 3 woods — large growth but inferior/porous and not durable
rubrics_metrics.description: "All those trees of finer growth and nobler dimensions, the quality of which is inferior, and apparently not of a durable character—of this class are Nos. 7, 13, 20, 23, and 24."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even though these trees produce large timbers (examples: 35–45 ft; 36 ft; 30 ft; 40–60 ft), their porosity, lightness, and apparent liability to decay make them unsuitable for long-lived naval applications without further evidence of durability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Class 4 woods — good quality meeting minimum naval length requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: "The woods of good quality which just attain in their growth the minimum of length which would fit them for naval purposes—these are Nos. 12, 17, 21, and 22."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the most promising for shipbuilding if greater lengths can be obtained in quantity; inspector discusses Taxa, Mocosso-cosso, Páo-fava, Metteral as potentially suitable substitutes for African oak or mahogany, subject to availability of larger sizes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dimension / length and section requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Timber is evaluated by reported lengths and square dimensions (e.g., "twenty feet in length, and twenty inches square"; "thirty-five to forty-five feet in length, and from three to four feet square").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific minimum lengths and section sizes determine whether a wood can be used for keels, beams, masts, planks, futtocks, tiers of wheels. Inspector repeatedly notes that increased length/size is needed to make a wood valuable for beams, planks, masts, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific gravity / density as an indicator of quality
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspector records specific gravities (e.g., Taxa ~67 lbs, Mocosso-cosso ~59 lbs, Panguira ~53 lbs, Mugunda ~38 lbs) and uses them to infer weight, grain closeness, and durability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Higher specific gravity is associated with closer grain, heaviness, and better appearance for naval/cabinet use; low specific gravity may indicate light, porous, and inferior quality. Use as one quantitative metric alongside others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grain closeness, colour, and apparent durability
rubrics_metrics.description: Woods described as "close in the grain, heavy, of a reddish colour, and apparently of good and durable character" (Taxa) versus "yellowish in colour, porous, and inferior in quality" (several large-growth woods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Close grain and favourable colouration (and heaviness) are positive signs for ship- and cabinet- work; porous, yellowish woods are viewed as inferior and liable to decay.

rubrics_metrics.name: Porosity and susceptibility to decay
rubrics_metrics.description: A recurring criterion: woods described as "porous, and inferior in quality" are judged not durable and unsuitable for naval purposes despite large size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Porosity undermines durability in marine environments; even large timbers that are porous should be treated with caution and require further evidence before adoption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Straight growth and natural curvature (shapes for specific uses)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspector notes straightness ("straight growth") and also remarks on degree of natural curvature ("The degree of natural curvature in the growth of the frame timbers could not be ascertained").
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Straight growth favors masts, beams, and long spars; natural curvature is relevant for frames and knees. Ability to procure pieces with appropriate natural shapes is part of suitability assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Surface qualities: ability to take a high polish and suitability for cabinet-work
rubrics_metrics.description: Woods noted to "take a high polish" or to "resemble mahogany in its grain" are recommended for cabinet-work and joinery (e.g., Mocosso-cosso, Páo-ferro, Páo-fava, Metteral).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a wood can be polished and resembles mahogany, it may substitute for mahogany in furniture and interior work; suitability depends on sample appearance and quantities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resistance to marine borers (Teredo navalis) and other specific environmental resistances
rubrics_metrics.description: Report: "Red Tacamaca and Colofan are impervious to the Teredo Navalis" (Madagascar woods).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resistance to shipworms and marine borers is a decisive quality for hull planking and underwater timbers; such properties significantly increase a wood's value for shipbuilding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compatibility with metal fittings (non-corroding properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statement: "sandal-wood and ebony—also a very valuable wood; iron and steel instruments inserted in which will not corrode."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Woods that do not corrode iron/steel fastenings are advantageous for durable ship and tool construction; note this property when selecting woods for areas with metal fixings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-structural utilitarian properties (dyeing, quinine, tallow, oils)
rubrics_metrics.description: Inspector and catalogue note uses such as quinine from bark ("from the bark of this tree quinine is extracted"), dyeing properties ("dyes cotton, silk, and wool that colour"), and extraction of oil/tallow used medically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond structural uses, woods and bark may have chemical/industrial value (dyes, medicinal quinine, tallow). These properties affect economic valuation and potential separate markets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical procurement and trial criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Requests and guidance: determine "what steps you would recommend should be taken for obtaining a supply of these descriptions of timber, and for conveying the same to England"; need "further information... whether greater lengths are procurable, and as to the quantities to be found in the forests; if these are easy obtainable in large quantities, and they can be brought readily to a port for shipment, they would be deserving of a trial in our dock-yards."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decision to adopt foreign woods depends not only on material properties but on supply chain feasibility: existence of larger lengths, sufficient quantities, ease/cost of transport to port, and ability to procure logs for trial use in dockyards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vessel timber condition inspection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: From inspection of the ship 'Thomas Blyth': timber/planking appear "in sound and good condition"; wood "of a chocolate colour, close, hard, and somewhat stringy in its texture, and free from shakes." Scantlings and lengths were recorded (e.g., nine to twelve inches, beams ~26 ft).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: On-vessel inspection uses current physical condition (soundness, absence of shakes), visible grain/texture, and existing scantlings to judge long-term fitness; small scantlings may signal limited applicability to larger warships but indicate suitability for small vessels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Historical localization / evidentiary criteria (case: position of Ophir)
rubrics_metrics.description: For locating ancient place names, arguments assert that all articles listed in ancient cargoes should be procurable in the candidate country; translation evidence (Septuagint renderings), classical testimonies (Josephus), presence of characteristic products (pine-trees, precious stones), and known trade routes/colonies are used as evidence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When arguing for the identification of an ancient locale, combine archaeological/product congruence (was the cargo native to the region), philological evidence from translations, ancient historian testimony, and plausibility of trade-route logistics. Multiple lines strengthen a proposal; absence or incompatibility weakens it.
